name: Uva ursi (bearberry leaf, Arctostaphylos uva-ursi)
short: Hydroquinone exposure, not uva ursi: a fatal poisoning (title only), a child's seizures. Uva ursi: bull's-eye retinal damage after 3 years' use; kidney infection in 8 of 207 vs 2 of 191 on antibiotic.
text: Eye damage (case report): a 56-year-old woman who had taken uva ursi by mouth for 3 years noticed reduced visual acuity within the past year, and eye examination including fluorescein angiography showed a typical bull's-eye maculopathy (damage to the central retina) in both eyes; the authors note that uva ursi is a known inhibitor of melanin synthesis and say potential retinal toxic drugs should include it. Infections in trials: in a double-blind trial in 398 women with suspected uncomplicated urinary tract infection in 42 German family practices, 8 of 207 women developed pyelonephritis (kidney infection) when given uva ursi first compared with 2 of 191 given the antibiotic fosfomycin (p 0.067); other adverse events were similar between the groups, and the authors conclude that uva ursi reduced antibiotic use but led to a higher symptom burden and more safety concerns than fosfomycin. In a placebo-controlled trial in 382 women with symptoms of lower urinary tract infection, all of whom had a back-up antibiotic prescription, there were no safety concerns and no upper urinary tract infections were recorded. Hydroquinone: arbutin, the main constituent, is absorbed and converted in the liver to hydroquinone conjugates. A 2013 review of published and unpublished experimental and human studies, written in its own words to support the safety of therapeutic daily doses, estimated a permitted daily exposure for free hydroquinone from an experimental no-observed-effect level and states that there is no direct evidence from human data that free hydroquinone causes convulsions, liver or kidney toxicity, or tumour promotion in humans. Hydroquinone exposure, not uva ursi preparations: on the other side of that review sentence, case records of hydroquinone exposure name a death, hepatitis, a blood cancer and seizures; none of their titles or abstracts mentions uva ursi, and none shows what dose or route would be needed to cause harm. A 1966 report, available as a title only, has a title that begins 'A case of fatal poisoning by hydroquinone' and goes on to describe detecting hydroquinone in the viscera; the title does not say who was poisoned, by what route or from what source. A 2012 case report describes myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia (a blood cancer) in a 43-year-old man after 16 years of occupational exposure to hydroquinone in radiographic developer solution; the authors review hydroquinone as a potential cause of blood and lymphatic cancers, and a single case cannot show cause. A 1995 letter, available as a title only, is titled 'Darkroom hepatitis after exposure to hydroquinone'; the title does not give the route. A child developed status epilepticus (prolonged seizures) after swallowing a skin-lightening solution containing 2% hydroquinone, and the authors discuss hydroquinone's effects on the central nervous system (case report); the abstract notes that such products may also contain heavy metals and corticosteroids, and does not list this product's other ingredients. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
